## Overview

The Opata are an Indigenous people in Mexico whose traditional territory, the Opatería, encompassed the mountainous northeast and central part of Sonora, extending near the border with the United States. Their towns were concentrated in the river valleys of the San Miguel, Sonora, Moctezuma, Bavispe, and Aros rivers, where they practiced irrigated agriculture. At Spanish contact in the 16th century, they were the most numerous people in Sonora, with population estimates for the Opatería ranging from 20,000 to 70,000. The Opata language was Uto-Aztecan and closely related to Eudeve, O'odham, Tarahumara, Tepehuan, Yaqui, and Mayo. The language is now extinct or inactive, although a revitalization effort began with the Opata Living Dictionary in 2021. Opata material and intangible culture included irrigation agriculture, cotton weaving, adobe architecture, hunting, fishing, ritual beverages, music, masks, and processions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Cotton fiber dresses* — Opata women wove dyed, full-length, colorful dresses from cotton fiber.

*Serapes* — Men wore serapes, described as shawls used in cold weather.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Opata textile motifs or pattern vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

Opata women wore dyed, full-length, colorful cotton-fiber dresses and were described as skilled weavers. In warm weather, women often wore hide skirts similar to those of men. Men generally dressed more scantily in skirts made of hide, while both sexes could go nude during the hot season. Men also wore serapes, or shawls, in cold weather. Footwear consisted of sandals made from hide. Necklaces and other adornments made from hide, stone, bone, shell, and feathers were worn by both sexes. Clothing practices changed substantially after Spanish colonization: by 1800, the Opata commonly spoke Spanish, followed Christianity, and were largely assimilated into Spanish society. Carl Lumholtz later described the Opatas as dressing like Mexicans and as being merged with the laboring class of Mexico through intermarriage.

### Architecture

Opata settlements were organized in river valleys and, during the statelet period, included central towns surrounded by satellite communities, hamlets, and rancherías. A central town had at least 200 two- and three-story adobe houses, with a population of six per house or 1,200 or more. Hamlets contained 9 to 25 houses, while rancherías had fewer than 9 houses. Ordinary dwellings consisted of thatched huts and small houses made of adobe and zacate with thatched roofs. During warm, dry seasons, semi-subterranean dwellings known as a *hu'uki* were also used. Hu'ukis could serve as sweat lodges, and small ones were built for storing legumes so that they remained cool and fresh for longer.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do record iron use: according to Opata oral traditionalists, the name “Opata” means “iron people,” because iron ore was abundant in Opata territory and Opata spear tips were made from iron ore. Everyday subsistence tools included bows and arrows for hunting deer, spears and nets for fishing, canal-irrigation works, and agricultural fields. Other household objects included hand-held gourd rattles, bands of small ankle rattles, hand-held drums, and masks carved from Cottonwood.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Opata people wore necklaces and other adornments made from hide, stone, bone, shell, and feathers. The sources also describe the Jova chieftain Sisibotari wearing a becoming marten skin on the wrist of his left hand, the hand that held the bow when shooting an arrow.

## Music & performance

The sources document instruments used in the Opata spring procession rite known today as the *fariseo*. These instruments include hand-held gourd rattles, bands of small ankle rattles, and hand-held drums. The rite is practiced during Easter week in most towns and villages in Opata Country and incorporates some Catholicism. Masks used in the procession often include traditional masks carved from Cottonwood and depicting painted human and animal-like facial figures.

The sources also describe *tanori*, a fermented maize atole beverage, as part of ceremonial and celebratory life. It was normally drunk during certain ceremonies and celebrations, and expert preparers sometimes took Tanori as a second name.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name a fertility rite described in Spanish priests’ written accounts as a round dance known as the “Mariachi.” They also describe the spring procession rite known as the *fariseo*, practiced during Easter week and involving masks, gourd rattles, ankle rattles, and hand-held drums.

## Festivals & rituals

The Opata spring procession rite known today as the *fariseo* is still exercised during Easter week in most towns and villages in Opata Country. It includes masks, traditional Opatan instruments, and some Catholicism. Masks may be carved from Cottonwood and painted with human or animal-like facial figures.

The sources also record fertility rites. One commonly reported rite was a round dance known as the “Mariachi,” which Spanish priests’ written accounts described as “obscene.” The fermented maize beverage *tanori* was normally drunk during certain ceremonies and celebrations.

## Foodways

The Opata depended upon agriculture for much of their subsistence. Principal crops were maize, beans, squash, and cotton. Because rainfall was scarce and irregular, they practiced canal irrigation as well as dry-land farming. Early Spanish explorers described large and productive fields among the Opata.

Opata people also hunted game, especially deer, with bows and arrows; fished in rivers with spears and nets; and gathered wild foods such as Chenopodium and cactus leaves and fruits. They produced a fermented maize atole beverage known as *tanori*, which was associated with certain ceremonies and celebrations.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources mention Opata oral traditionalists in connection with explanations of the name “Opata” and the name Joylraua. According to these oral traditionalists, “Opata” was used by some Tehuima villages for themselves and meant “iron people,” while Joylraua was the name of an ancient Eudeve village named after an honored chieftain. These accounts differ from missionary and anthropological explanations.

The sources also preserve a historical description of the Jova chieftain Sisibotari by Father Andrés Pérez de Ribas. Sisibotari was known throughout Opata country and acted as an intermediary between the Opatan peoples and the Spanish. Contemporary preservation efforts include the first-ever Opata Living Dictionary, launched in 2021 by the Fundación OPATA-TEGUIMA in collaboration with the Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages.

## Language & religion

Opata was a Uto-Aztecan language closely related to Eudeve. Related and associated varieties included Eudeve, Dohema, Tehuima, and Jova. The Eudeve dialect was called Dohema; the Tehuimas spoke Tehuima; and the Jovas spoke Jova. Eudeve and Tehuima were closely related, while Jova was more distinct. Ópata was also known as Tegüima, Teguima, Tehuima, Tehui, Tonichi, Sonori, and Ure. The language was believed to be dead by 1930, and the INALI does not count Opata among the currently extant Indigenous languages of Mexico. The Opata Nation considers the language inactive and is undertaking revitalization.

By 1800, the Opata were mostly followers of Christianity and commonly spoke Spanish. Catholic practices became associated with Opata processions, including the fariseo.
